newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian shares rally on finance minister's statement.
newsitem.headline: Indian shares rally on finance minister's statement.

text.p: Indian shares rallied in hectic trade on Monday after the finance minister said that a controversial new tax on companies may soon be phased out, dealers and analysts said.
"This bit of good news is a tonic for the markets," said Antony Sequeira, managing director at Arcadia Share & Stock Brokers.
The Bombay Stock Exchange's (BSE) top 30-share index jumped 63.10 points, or 2.19 percent, to 2,944.25 in afternoon trade on Monday, with blue chips leading the rally in share prices.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on Sunday said that a minimum corporate tax may be phased out after a new Income Tax Act and Companies Act came into force.

"The introduction of MAT (Minimum Alternate Tax) in the last budget has caused a high degree of discomfort to industry. It was introduced as a number of companies were paying dividend but not tax," Chidambaram told a recent seminar organised by the International Association of Lawyers, newspapers reported on Monday.
Dealers said the news about the MAT came at a time when the markets were over-sold, with investor sentiment at rock-bottom.
"The gains recorded by prices will be sustainable at least for some time...," said Ulhas Paymaster, a BSE broker.

"While in the past the government had overlooked the consequences of imposing MAT, it now seems that it would seriously review the same," brokerage firm Khandwala Securities said in its weekly report.
The new tax introduced in July by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government was aimed at high-growth firms that avoided paying taxes by putting profits into new projects or expansions.
"MAT will definitely not go away, but there might be a simplification," Paymaster said.

Last week, Deve Gowda told industrialists in New Delhi he would review the recently introduced tax in "next year's budget," which the industrialists told him was the cause of slowing industrial growth and corporate profits.
The benchark BSE index jumped about five percent the next day. India's budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) is normally presented to Parliament in the last week of February.
Analysts expect a short-term uptrend in the market with alarm bells finally ringing in New Delhi.
"There is still some confusion about MAT, but the market is now convinced that the government is concerned about the slump in the bourses," Sequeira said.
Bombay stocks, which fell to a three-year low in the first week of December, are down about 28 percent from the year's high of 4,069 on June 18.
